metadata.title: Engagement, achievement, and teacher classroom practices in mathematics: Insights from TIMSS 2011 and PISA 2012

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2011 and PISA 2012 microdata and applies complex survey weighting to obtain population-representative parameter estimates. For TIMSS 2011, estimates are weighted using the student sampling weight totwgt and variance estimation uses jackknife replication weights; for PISA 2012, estimates are weighted using W_FSTUWT and variance estimation uses balanced repeated replication (BRR) weights. The analytic unit is the student (single-level SEM), justified by low school-level variance (ICC mostly < 0.05) and design constraints that limit multilevel modeling. For PISA, because engagement and teacher-practice items are in the rotated part of the questionnaire, inferential analyses are restricted to the subset of students who responded to the rotated items; rotation design is treated as missing at random and does not affect reporting proportions or replicate-weight computation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study focuses on eighth graders in TIMSS 2011 and 15-year-old students in PISA 2012, but restricts analyses to four focal education systems: Australia, Finland, Romania, and Singapore. For PISA 2012, engagement and teacher-classroom-practice measures are administered in the rotated part of the student questionnaire; therefore, path analyses are conducted on the subset of students who completed the rotated questionnaire items (missingness due to rotation is treated as missing at random). For TIMSS 2011, engagement items have <5% missingness and are listwise deleted in subsequent analyses. Teacher classroom-practice items in TIMSS 2011 have substantial missingness in Australia due to low teacher response rate; these teacher-practice variables are multiply imputed (m=5) and then included in the path analysis for Australia. For PISA 2012, teacher-practice items are student-reported and missingness is largely due to rotation design rather than nonresponse.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics (achievement levels; engagement CFA + path analysis)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM path analysis (standardized coefficients, weighted by totwgt); model fit: RMSEA range 0.04–0.07 and CFI range 0.95–0.98 across countries (Singapore, Finland, Australia, Romania).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics the study leveraged socioeconomic status (SES), teacher classroom challenge, teacher classroom structure, teacher classroom support, and gender to model mathematics achievement levels, finding that SES was a consistently strong positive predictor of achievement (β = 0.32–0.50 across countries) while teacher-reported classroom practices showed limited or selective associations (e.g., challenge positively associated with achievement in Finland, Australia, and Romania; structure/support mostly null). This indicates that, in these TIMSS contexts, equity-oriented policies that address socioeconomic disparities may be more impactful for mathematics achievement than broad increases in generic instructional practice frequency alone, though appropriately challenging instruction may still matter in some systems.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Mathematics (mathematical literacy achievement levels; engagement CFA + path analysis)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM path analysis (standardized coefficients, weighted by W_FSTUWT); model fit: RMSEA range 0.04–0.06 and CFI range 0.93–0.99 across countries (Singapore, Finland, Australia, Romania).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics the study leveraged socioeconomic status (SES), teacher classroom challenge, teacher classroom structure, teacher classroom support, and gender to model mathematics achievement levels, finding that SES was again a strong positive predictor (β = 0.29–0.42 across countries) while student-reported teacher practices were more consequential and heterogeneous (e.g., challenge negatively associated with achievement across countries; structure positively associated with achievement in Finland and Australia; support mostly null). This indicates that improving classroom practices may relate to achievement more strongly when practices are captured from students, but the direction of effects—especially for challenge—suggests that “more challenge” is not uniformly beneficial and may require calibration to student readiness and context.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics (engagement CFA + path analysis)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM path analysis (standardized coefficients, weighted by totwgt); R2 for interest: Singapore 0.00, Finland 0.03, Australia 0.03, Romania 0.02.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics the study leveraged teacher classroom structure, support, challenge, socioeconomic status (SES), and gender to predict interest in mathematics, finding that teacher-reported classroom practices showed little to no association with interest across countries while SES was a consistent positive predictor (e.g., β = 0.06 in Singapore; β = 0.16–0.15 in Finland/Australia; β = 0.10 in Romania) and gender effects were limited. This indicates that, in TIMSS, students’ interest is more strongly patterned by background than by the measured frequency of generic instructional practices, implying that engagement interventions may need to combine instructional improvements with supports that address socioeconomic constraints.

main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM path analysis (standardized coefficients, weighted by W_FSTUWT); R2 for interest: Singapore 0.14, Finland 0.19, Australia 0.21, Romania 0.03.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics the study leveraged teacher classroom structure, support, challenge, socioeconomic status (SES), and gender to predict interest in mathematics, finding that teacher-reported practices were more strongly related to interest in most systems (e.g., structure and support positively associated with interest in Singapore, Finland, and Australia) while challenge was largely null except a positive association in Romania (β = 0.19). SES showed a small negative association with interest in Singapore (β = −0.05) and a positive association in Finland (β = 0.13), indicating cross-country heterogeneity. This indicates that engagement may be more responsive to classroom practice when students report instructional experiences, but the SES–engagement relationship can reverse by context, so interventions should be locally tailored rather than assumed to be universally beneficial.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics and PISA 2012 Mathematics to examine how emotional/cognitive engagement (interest, self-concept, future utility beliefs) relates to teacher classroom practices and mathematics achievement across four focal systems (Singapore, Finland, Australia, Romania). The authors estimate CFA measurement models for engagement and then fit path models separately by country, using robust WLS in Mplus for ordinal indicators. Teacher classroom practices are measured as composites of structure, support, and challenge, reported by teachers in TIMSS 2011 and by students in PISA 2012, while achievement is modeled using mathematics achievement levels derived from PVs (continuous scores were not used due to nonconvergence). Survey weights are applied (totwgt with jackknife for TIMSS; W_FSTUWT with BRR for PISA), and PISA analyses are restricted to the rotated questionnaire subset. Results show SES is a consistently strong positive predictor of achievement, while instructional practices have weaker and more heterogeneous associations—especially for “challenge,” which is positive in some TIMSS contexts but negative for achievement in PISA. The study is cross-sectional, so associations cannot be interpreted causally, and differences in measurement source (teacher vs student) may contribute to contrasting patterns.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This paper is not an empirical machine-learning prediction study: it uses structural equation modeling (CFA and path analysis) rather than training/evaluating ML algorithms. Consequently, ml_techniques is intentionally empty and no ML performance metrics (e.g., AUC/RMSE from predictive models) are applicable. The extraction focuses on the reported SEM path coefficients and model fit indices as the substantive results.
